simulation.title: Parlington Ltd — Enterprise AWS Cloud Transformation
simulation.description: You are the Senior AWS Solutions Architect hired to lead Parlington Ltd's full cloud transformation. Assess 120 servers and 42 applications, design a multi-account AWS Landing Zone, build Terraform IaC, deploy a production EKS platform with four microservices, establish DevSecOps pipelines, design an enterprise data platform, plan a six-wave migration with DR, and present to the Architecture Review Board in Week 36. The FCA is already pursuing enforcement action. The board is watching.

company.name: Parlington Ltd
company.about: Parlington Ltd is a UK asset management firm (£4.2bn AUM) regulated by the FCA and PRA, undergoing a board-mandated cloud transformation to AWS. The firm is 14 months overdue on FCA Operational Resilience compliance and faces up to £8.7M in penalties if transformation fails.

inbox_messages.subject: Welcome to Parlington — we need you to hit the ground running
inbox_messages.body:
Welcome aboard.

I'll be direct with you: this programme is already behind where it should be. Craig Whitfield left us two weeks ago with incomplete handover notes. The FCA has written to us twice. The board gave me 18 months to fix this and we've used two of them getting you through the door.

Your first priority is Phase 1 — a complete discovery of our estate. 120 servers, 42 applications, two data centres. I need to know what we're actually dealing with before I can tell the board anything credible.

The data files are in /docs/data/. Craig's handover notes are in /docs/process-notes.md. Read both carefully — there are things in those notes that will change how you approach the discovery.

I need your Discovery Assessment Report by end of Week 4. Not a slide deck. A proper document I can defend in front of Priya and Marcus.

One more thing: James Liu mentioned there may be a third FCA letter on its way. If it arrives before you finish Phase 1, it changes our timeline. I'll let you know.

Good luck. I mean that.

— Sarah

inbox_messages.subject: Phase 2 kickoff — Landing Zone design
inbox_messages.body:
Good work on the discovery.

Now we need to move fast on the Landing Zone. I've reviewed your Phase 1 output and I agree with your assessment. The single legacy AWS account is a liability — no SCPs, no CloudTrail, three public S3 buckets including one with Terraform state in it. Craig flagged that one in August. It still isn't fixed.

For Phase 2 I need:
- A multi-account structure design (ADR-001 needs completing)
- Control Tower configuration plan
- Governance framework including SCP strategy
- HLD AND LLD — Marcus and Priya both need to sign off the LLD before we order infrastructure

One thing I need you to watch: Marcus and Rachel are in disagreement about whether we need a separate Data OU. Marcus thinks it adds complexity. Rachel says Amara needs it for Lake Formation governance. I'm not going to adjudicate this for you — I want your architectural recommendation with a rationale.

Deadline: Week 8. The Landing Zone must be live before we touch networking.

— Sarah

inbox_messages.subject: Phase 3 — Networking and Security. Priya is watching this one closely.
inbox_messages.body:
The Landing Zone looks solid. Good work.

Phase 3 is where things get politically complicated. Priya Anand has asked to be briefed personally on the security architecture before it goes anywhere near the board. She is specifically worried about the 17 applications with no DR and the direct compliance gap with PS21/3.

Her exact words in our last 1:1: 'I want to see a risk register that names the risk, the owner, the FCA consequence, and the mitigation. Not a traffic light spreadsheet.'

For networking: the Direct Connect order has not been placed. Craig flagged this in his handover notes (OQ-002). This is now a programme-critical path item. I need you to document the architecture AND flag the ordering status explicitly in your submission.

The mystery IP range (10.200.0.0/16) also needs a decision in this phase — you can't design the VPC CIDR plan without resolving it.

Deadline: Week 12.

— Sarah

inbox_messages.subject: Phase 4 — IaC platform. Ben is expecting you.
inbox_messages.body:
Phase 3 sign-off from Priya received. Well done — that is not easy.

Phase 4: you are building the IaC platform. Ben Hartley is your closest collaborator on this phase. He has strong opinions on Terraform module design. Engage him early — he will push back on patterns he disagrees with, and he is usually right.

A few things I need you to know:

The Terraform modules in /terraform/ are partially complete and have known bugs. The CloudFormation template in /cloudformation/ has two errors. The Python scripts in /python/ are broken. Your job is to identify all issues, fix them, and extend them to production quality.

Marcus has asked for a FinOps cost report from the Python tooling by end of Phase 4. He wants to see actual AWS cost data, not estimates.

There is also an incident to investigate. At 02:14 on Monday morning, PAR-DB-012 (the PEMIS database server, 128 cores, £9,200/month) became unresponsive. Ben restarted it manually. It came back up but nobody knows why it failed. I need an incident report.

Deadline: Week 16.

— Sarah

inbox_messages.subject: Phase 5 — EKS platform. Rachel has been waiting for this.
inbox_messages.body:
IaC platform looks good. Ben is satisfied — that matters.

Phase 5 is the platform engineering phase. Rachel Thornton has been asking about EKS since her first week. She has a vision for developer self-service with GitOps. David Osei wants central infrastructure control. You need to design a platform that satisfies both.

Four microservices to deploy: Customer Service, Payments Service, Notification Service, Audit Service. The starter manifests in /kubernetes/ have known issues — wrong ports, missing resource limits, no probes, single replicas. Fix them all.

The ArgoCD configuration in /kubernetes/gitops/ is not wired up. The repoURL is a placeholder. Fix this and demonstrate a working GitOps sync.

PCI-DSS note: the Payments Service is in-scope for cardholder data. It must be network-isolated from the other three services. Network policies required.

Deadline: Week 22.

— Sarah

inbox_messages.subject: Phase 6 — DevSecOps and Observability. The pipeline is broken.
inbox_messages.body:
EKS platform approved. Good work navigating the Rachel/David tension.

Phase 6: the GitHub Actions pipeline in /.github/workflows/deploy.yml is broken and has multiple security issues. I need you to identify every problem, fix them all, and extend the pipeline with proper DevSecOps controls.

Specifically: the pipeline currently uses long-lived AWS credentials. This is unacceptable for a regulated financial institution under FCA SS2/21. Replace with OIDC. Add SAST scanning, dependency vulnerability scanning, and container image scanning before any push to ECR.

For observability: I need SLI/SLO dashboards in Grafana for all four microservices. Priya has asked for a payments success rate SLO of 99.95%. If we miss that in production, it is an operational resilience event.

Deadline: Week 26.

— Sarah

inbox_messages.subject: ARB is Week 36. This is the most important presentation of the programme.
inbox_messages.body:
You have eight weeks until the Architecture Review Board.

The board consists of me (chair), Marcus (CFO), Priya (CRO), and two non-executive directors. One of the NEDs has an AWS background and will ask technical questions. The other is a pure finance NED and will ask about cost and risk.

What they will challenge:
- Why did we choose EKS over ECS or serverless?
- What is the DR strategy for the 17 applications that currently have none?
- How does the AI platform (Bedrock) fit into the FCA regulatory framework?
- What is the total cost of ownership at steady state vs the current £3.8M run-rate?
- What happens if we miss the data centre exit deadline in March 2026?

Your ARB pack must answer all of these before they ask.

Record your executive presentation. 12 minutes maximum. No jargon. The finance NED will not know what a VPC is.

The ARB Decision Log must capture every decision made, the alternatives considered, and the risks accepted.

This is what the whole programme has been building toward.

— Sarah

inbox_messages.subject: Hey — welcome. Few things Craig didn't mention.
inbox_messages.body:
Hi,

Ben here. Lead Infra Eng. Glad you're on board — Craig leaving was rough timing.

Few things you need to know that aren't in the handover notes:

1. The Terraform state bucket (parlington-terraform-state) has been publicly readable since March. I flagged it to Craig, he flagged it to David, nothing happened. Block public access TODAY before anything else.

2. The /terraform/vpc/main.tf has a CIDR bug. Default is 172.16.0.0/16. That will conflict with our on-prem space if you follow Craig's recommendation to use 172.16.0.0/12 for AWS. You need to agree the CIDR plan with David and me before touching Terraform.

3. PAR-DB-012 — the big PEMIS database server — has been flaky for weeks. The monthly_cost_gbp in the estate CSV is £9,200 for it, which is accurate, but what the CSV doesn't tell you is it's running at 94% CPU utilisation on average. It's been like that since June. Nobody's escalated it because nobody wanted to be the person who said the most expensive server is also the most overloaded one.

4. The dependency delimiters in the app portfolio CSV are inconsistent — I did part of that spreadsheet and used semicolons, Rachel's team used commas, and somebody else used pipes. Sorry about that. Normalise before you analyse.

Anything else you need — I'm on Teams. Don't email me, I don't check it.

— Ben

inbox_messages.subject: The CloudFormation template has two bugs — want me to walk you through them?
inbox_messages.body:
For Phase 4 — the security-baseline.yaml in /cloudformation/ has two issues I spotted when Craig first committed it:

Bug 1 (syntax): Line with 'CloudWatchLogsLogGroupArnRef' — that property name doesn't exist. Should be 'CloudWatchLogsLogGroupArn'. The stack will fail to deploy with a cryptic error if you don't fix this first.

Bug 2 (logic): GuardDuty FindingPublishingFrequency is set to SIX_HOURS. Priya's security policy requires FIFTEEN_MINUTES for production. She will catch this in review. Fix it before you submit.

Also — the inventory.py script in /python/ will throw a KeyError on any server that has no tags at all. There are a few in the estate like that. Use instance.get('Tags', []) not instance['Tags'].

Want me to pair with you on the Terraform module design? I have opinions on the state backend setup.

— Ben

inbox_messages.subject: Risk register requirements — non-negotiable
inbox_messages.body:
I understand Phase 3 covers security and networking.

I want to be clear about what I need from the risk register before I will sign off this phase:

1. Every risk must name a specific FCA/PRA regulatory reference (e.g. PS21/3, SS2/21, SYSC 13)
2. Every risk must name an owner by role title (not just 'team')
3. Every risk affecting the 17 applications with no DR must have a specific remediation milestone tied to a programme phase
4. The risk register must include a column for 'SMCR accountable individual' — I need to know who is personally liable for each risk

I also need you to note something in your security architecture: the three public S3 buckets in the legacy account (including the Terraform state file) represent a potential data breach. If personal data was exposed — and I don't yet know whether it was — this may need to be reported to the ICO under UK GDPR Article 33 within 72 hours of our becoming aware. James Liu and the DPO need to be involved.

I am not the villain here. I am trying to protect the firm and the individuals who are personally accountable under SMCR.

— Priya Anand
Chief Risk Officer

inbox_messages.subject: RE: DR architecture — I need a decision
inbox_messages.body:
I have just come out of a budget meeting with Marcus.

He wants to defer the DR architecture work to Phase 8. His argument: it costs money now and the FCA hasn't formally enforced yet.

My position: we are already 14 months overdue on PS21/3. APP-001 (PEMIS), APP-002 (OMS), APP-003 (CRP), and APP-004 (RRG) all have P1 criticality and no DR whatsoever. In the last 12 weeks we have had 5 P1 incidents. The Week 12 incident (CRP and OMS simultaneously) lasted 6.7 hours. The FCA's impact tolerance for IBS-001 (Trade Execution) is 4 hours. We breached it.

I need your architectural recommendation: can DR for the top 4 P1 Critical applications be addressed in Phase 3 (baseline DR design) with full implementation in Phase 8? Or do we need to start implementation now?

This is not a political question. Give me the data.

— Priya

inbox_messages.subject: Cost model — I need numbers before I will approve Phase 2
inbox_messages.body:
I've been told you're pulling together the discovery report.

Before I approve budget release for Phase 2, I need to see a cost model in your Phase 1 output. Specifically:

1. Current total monthly infrastructure cost (from the estate data — not estimates)
2. Projected AWS cost at steady state
3. The annual licence savings we can achieve (Oracle alone is £340k/year)
4. Payback period on the £2.4M programme investment
5. A breakdown of where the infrastructure spend is going — by tier, not by OS

I have a theory that the database tier is eating a disproportionate share of the infrastructure budget. If your analysis confirms this, it changes the migration prioritisation and the ROI calculation.

Note: I am aware that Priya wants to start DR work immediately. I understand the regulatory position. But I need to see the cost model first before I agree to front-load that cost in Phase 3.

Numbers. Not slides. Not narratives. Numbers.

— Marcus

inbox_messages.subject: FinOps — this needs to be built into the platform, not bolted on later
inbox_messages.body:
I've been thinking about the FinOps framework.

I don't want a monthly spreadsheet. I want:

1. Cost Explorer configured with cost allocation tags (Environment, CostCentre, Team, DataClassification) applied to EVERY resource from day one
2. Budget alerts at 80% and 100% of monthly allocation per account
3. A weekly cost report generated automatically by the Python tooling — not manually by someone
4. Savings Plans and Reserved Instance recommendations reviewed quarterly
5. Any resource without a CostCentre tag flagged automatically and escalated to the team owner within 48 hours

The target is £1.9M annual run-rate. I am holding you to that figure.

If we overspend by more than 10% in any quarter, I will want a full cost review before releasing further programme budget.

— Marcus

tools.name: AWS Free Tier
tools.purpose: Primary cloud platform for all architecture work. Free Tier covers EC2 t2.micro, S3 (5GB), Lambda (1M requests), CloudWatch, IAM, VPC, and many other services used in this simulation.
signup_steps: Go to aws.amazon.com/free and click 'Create a Free Account'
Enter your email address and choose an AWS account name (e.g. 'parlington-simulation')
Provide payment details (required for account creation — Free Tier will not charge you for covered services)
Complete identity verification via phone
Choose the Basic Support plan (free)
Sign in to the AWS Console and set the region to eu-west-2 (London) using the top-right dropdown

tools.name: Terraform (HashiCorp)
tools.purpose: Industry-standard IaC tool used by the majority of UK enterprise AWS environments. Used in Phase 4 to fix, extend, and deploy the Parlington VPC and IAM modules.
signup_steps: Go to developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/install
Select your operating system and follow the installation instructions
Verify installation: open a terminal and run 'terraform --version'
Clone the parlington-cloud-transformation repository to your local machine
Navigate to the /terraform directory — this is your working directory for Phase 4
Run 'terraform init' to initialise (note: backend config must be completed first)

tools.name: Draw.io (diagrams.net)
tools.purpose: Free diagramming tool with built-in AWS architecture icon library. Used across all phases to produce HLD, LLD, network diagrams, security architecture, and data platform architecture.
signup_steps: Go to app.diagrams.net — no account required
Click 'Create New Diagram'
Select 'Network' or 'AWS' from the template categories
To get AWS icons: click the '+' shape panel button, search 'AWS', enable the AWS shape library
Save your diagrams to Google Drive or GitHub for submission evidence
Export as PNG or SVG for submission: File → Export As → PNG

tools.name: GitHub
tools.purpose: All evidence must be committed to the parlington-cloud-transformation repository. GitHub Actions is used in Phase 6 for CI/CD pipeline work.
signup_steps: Go to github.com/signup and create a free account
Fork the parlington-cloud-transformation repository to your account
Clone your fork locally: `git clone [github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/parlington-cloud-transformation](https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/parlington-cloud-transformation)`
Create a branch for each phase: git checkout -b feature/phase-1-discovery
Commit your evidence to the correct directory after each phase
Open a pull request to main when each phase is complete

tools.name: Docker Desktop
tools.purpose: Build and test container images locally before pushing to ECR. Required for Phase 5 microservices work.
signup_steps: Go to docker.com/products/docker-desktop and download for your OS
Install Docker Desktop and start the application
Verify installation: run 'docker --version' in a terminal
Sign up for a free Docker Hub account at hub.docker.com
Test with: docker run hello-world

tools.name: Grafana Cloud (Free Tier)
tools.purpose: Build monitoring dashboards with SLI/SLO tracking. Free tier includes 10,000 metrics series, 50GB logs, and unlimited dashboards.
signup_steps: Go to grafana.com/auth/sign-up/create-user
Sign up with your email — choose the Free plan
Create a new Grafana stack (give it a name like 'parlington-monitoring')
Note your Grafana URL (format: [your-stack.grafana.net](https://YOUR-STACK.grafana.net))
For Phase 6: connect CloudWatch as a data source using your AWS credentials
Build dashboards using the requirements in the Phase 6 observability section

tools.name: Python + Boto3
tools.purpose: AWS SDK for Python. Used in Phase 4 to fix and extend the inventory, cost reporting, and compliance audit scripts in /python/.
signup_steps: Download Python 3.11+ from python.org/downloads
Install and verify: python3 --version
Install Boto3: pip3 install boto3
Configure AWS credentials: aws configure (enter your Access Key ID and Secret)
Test: python3 -c "import boto3; print(boto3.__version__)"
Navigate to /python/ in the repository — this is your working directory for Phase 4

tools.name: Amazon Bedrock
tools.purpose: AWS managed foundation model service. Used in Phase 9 to design the Parlington RAG architecture. Free tier available for certain models.
signup_steps: Sign in to AWS Console and navigate to Amazon Bedrock
Click 'Model access' in the left navigation
Request access to Anthropic Claude and Amazon Titan models (approval is instant for most)
Navigate to 'Playgrounds' to test prompts before designing the architecture
Note: Bedrock charges per token — keep test usage minimal (estimated < $1 for this phase)
Use the Bedrock API documentation for the RAG architecture design

content.headline: Lead a £2.4M AWS cloud transformation for an FCA-regulated asset manager before enforcement action hits
content.description: Parlington Ltd manages £4.2 billion in assets and is 14 months overdue on FCA Operational Resilience compliance. You are the Senior AWS Solutions Architect. 120 servers. 42 applications. Two data centres to exit by March 2026. A board that has already watched one transformation fail. This is the real thing.
content.employer_context: Senior AWS Solutions Architect roles in UK financial services require candidates who can demonstrate end-to-end enterprise transformation experience — not just individual service knowledge. This simulation mirrors the exact scope of real AWS transformation programmes at firms like KPMG, Accenture, Deloitte, and in-house at Lloyds, Barclays, and HSBC.

content.about: Parlington Ltd is a mid-tier UK asset management firm with £4.2 billion AUM, regulated by the FCA and PRA. Founded in 1994, the firm operates across UK equities, fixed income, multi-asset strategies, and institutional custody. A failed 2022 cloud transformation programme (£1.1M spent, zero production workloads migrated) left the board deeply cautious. A new CTO joined in January 2024 with a mandate to fix it in 18 months.
content.your_role: You are the Senior AWS Solutions Architect — the most senior technical hire on the programme. You report to the CTO (Sarah Nkemdirim) and are accountable to the Architecture Review Board. Every architecture decision from Landing Zone design to AI platform architecture goes through you. You will produce HLDs, LLDs, ADRs, a migration strategy, a FinOps framework, and an executive ARB presentation.
content.fun_fact: Parlington's FCA fine exposure is up to £8.7 million (10% of annual revenue) if the Operational Resilience compliance breach continues. The board approved this programme specifically to prevent that outcome.

content.intro_text: You will be working closely with these four people throughout the programme. Each has a different agenda. Learning to navigate their competing priorities is as important as the technical architecture work.

team_members.bio: Joined Parlington in January 2024, hired specifically to fix the failed 2022 cloud programme. Direct, data-driven, zero tolerance for vagueness. She has a mandate from the board and 16 months left to deliver. She will back you when you're right and challenge you when she thinks you're wrong. Do not surprise her with bad news.

Knows the Parlington estate better than anyone. Started the Terraform modules that are in the repository — they have bugs, and he knows it. Has strong opinions on IaC design patterns. Will push back on approaches he disagrees with, and he is usually right. Engage him early in Phase 4.

Personally accountable under SMCR for Parlington's FCA Operational Resilience compliance. She is not being difficult — she is managing her own regulatory liability. She needs specificity: risk IDs, regulatory references, named owners, and remediation milestones tied to programme phases. Give her that and she will sign off quickly.

Watches the programme budget on a weekly basis. The £2.4M ceiling is hard — no contingency release without his approval. His theory about the database tier cost is correct (you will prove it in Phase 1). He and Priya are in direct conflict about the timing of DR work. You will need data to resolve that conflict.

sections.title: Tools You Will Use — Set Up Now

content.text:
## Set up your tools before Phase 2

All tools below are free. Set them up now — some phases require tools to be ready before you start.

---

## 1. AWS Free Tier — Used in Phases 2–9

**Sign up:** [aws.amazon.com/free](https://aws.amazon.com/free/)

1. Click **Create a Free Account**
2. Enter your email and choose an account name (e.g. `parlington-simulation`)
3. Add payment details (required — Free Tier won't charge for covered services)
4. Complete phone verification
5. Choose **Basic Support** (free)
6. Set your region to **eu-west-2 (London)** in the top-right dropdown

> 💡 Set up now. Phase 2 starts in AWS.

---

## 2. GitHub — Used in All Phases

**Sign up:** [github.com/signup](https://github.com/signup)

1. Create a free GitHub account
2. Fork the **parlington-cloud-transformation** repository
3. Clone your fork locally: `git clone [https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/parlington-cloud-transformation](https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/parlington-cloud-transformation)`
4. You will commit evidence to this repository in every phase

> 💡 Fork the repo before Phase 1 ends.

---

## 3. Draw.io — Used in Phases 1, 2, 3, 7, 8, 9

**Open:** [app.diagrams.net](https://app.diagrams.net) — no account needed

1. Click **Create New Diagram**
2. Enable AWS shape library: click the **+** in the shape panel, search **AWS**, enable it
3. Save diagrams to GitHub or Google Drive
4. Export as PNG for submissions: **File → Export As → PNG**

> 💡 Open it now and create a blank diagram to confirm it works.

---

## 4. Terraform — Used in Phase 4

**Download:** [developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/install](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/install)

1. Install for your OS and run `terraform --version` to confirm
2. Navigate to `/terraform` in your cloned repository
3. You will fix and extend the modules already there

> 💡 Install before Phase 4. You do not need it yet.

---

## 5. Docker Desktop — Used in Phases 5, 6

**Download:** [docker.com/products/docker-desktop](https://www.docker.com/products/docker-desktop/)

1. Install and run `docker --version` to confirm
2. Sign up for a free Docker Hub account at [hub.docker.com](https://hub.docker.com)

> 💡 Install before Phase 5.

---

## 6. Grafana Cloud Free — Used in Phase 6

**Sign up:** [grafana.com/auth/sign-up/create-user](https://grafana.com/auth/sign-up/create-user)

1. Choose the **Free** plan
2. Create a stack named `parlington-monitoring`
3. Note your Grafana URL (format: `[https://YOUR-STACK.grafana.net](https://YOUR-STACK.grafana.net)`)

> 💡 Sign up before Phase 6.

---

## 7. Python + Boto3 — Used in Phase 4

**Download:** [python.org/downloads](https://www.python.org/downloads/)

1. Install Python 3.11+ and run `python3 --version`
2. Install Boto3: `pip3 install boto3`
3. Configure AWS credentials: `aws configure`

> 💡 Install before Phase 4.

Start with the OU structure. A standard FCA-regulated Landing Zone uses: Security OU (Audit + Log Archive accounts), Infrastructure OU (Shared Services account), Workloads OU with Production, NonProd, and Sandbox sub-OUs. For the Data OU question — Rachel is architecturally correct: Lake Formation governance requires account-level isolation. Recommend it with justification.

📋 EXPERT SAMPLE — OU structure:

ROOT (Management Account: parlington-management)
├── Security OU
│   ├── parlington-audit (CloudTrail, Config, SecurityHub aggregation)
│   └── parlington-log-archive (centralised S3 log storage, 7yr retention)
├── Infrastructure OU
│   └── parlington-shared-services (Transit Gateway, Route 53 Resolver, tooling)
├── Workloads OU
│   ├── Production OU
│   │   ├── parlington-payments-prod
│   │   ├── parlington-trading-prod
│   │   └── parlington-core-prod
│   ├── NonProd OU
│   │   ├── parlington-dev
│   │   └── parlington-test
│   └── Sandbox OU
│       └── parlington-innovation
└── Data Platform OU  ← RECOMMENDED (support Rachel's position)
    └── parlington-data-platform (Lake Formation, Glue, Redshift)

For the CIDR plan, avoid all 10.0.0.0/8 ranges (on-premises). Use 172.16.0.0/12 for AWS VPCs as Craig recommended, but allocate sub-ranges carefully to allow for expansion.

📋 EXPERT SAMPLE — CIDR allocation:

AWS CIDR Space: 172.16.0.0/12 (172.16.0.0 – 172.31.255.255)

Account allocations:
- Shared Services:     172.16.0.0/16
- Payments-Prod:       172.17.0.0/16
- Trading-Prod:        172.18.0.0/16
- Core-Prod:           172.19.0.0/16
- NonProd (Dev):       172.20.0.0/16
- NonProd (Test):      172.21.0.0/16
- Data Platform:       172.22.0.0/16

Production VPC subnet layout (172.17.0.0/16 example):
- Public subnets:   172.17.1.0/24, 172.17.2.0/24, 172.17.3.0/24 (3 AZs)
- Private subnets:  172.17.10.0/24, 172.17.11.0/24, 172.17.12.0/24
- Data subnets:     172.17.20.0/24, 172.17.21.0/24, 172.17.22.0/24
- TGW attach:       172.17.30.0/28, 172.17.30.16/28, 172.17.30.32/28

Complete the governance framework with the three SCPs and compliance mapping. Here is the full set of required content:

📋 EXPERT SAMPLE — SCPs and compliance mapping:

**SCP-001: Deny non-EU regions** (attached at root)
Effect: Deny all API calls where aws:RequestedRegion not in [eu-west-2, eu-west-1]
Exemptions: CloudFront, IAM, Route53, STS, WAF (global services)
Compliance: NCSC Cloud Principle 2 (Asset protection), UK GDPR (data residency)

**SCP-002: Require MFA for sensitive actions** (attached at root)
Effect: Deny iam:DeleteRole, s3:DeleteBucket, ec2:TerminateInstances unless aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent = true
Compliance: ISO 27001 A.9.4, FCA SYSC 13.7

**SCP-003: Prohibit public S3 buckets** (attached at Workloads OU)
Effect: Deny s3:PutBucketAcl and s3:PutBucketPolicy where condition allows public access
Compliance: ISO 27001 A.13.1, FCA SS2/21

**Mandatory tags:**
Environment: prod | nonprod | sandbox
CostCentre: [business unit code] — required for FinOps chargeback
DataClassification: RESTRICTED | CONFIDENTIAL | INTERNAL | PUBLIC
Team: [team name] — for operational ownership
ManagedBy: terraform | cloudformation | console (console requires approval)

Chosen because: automated guardrails prevent manual drift; account vending via Account Factory reduces provisioning from weeks to hours; native integration with AWS Security Hub, Config, and CloudTrail satisfies FCA SS2/21 audit requirements; SCPs applied at OU level provide inherited guardrails without per-account configuration.

deterministic_checks.failure_feedback: Change containerPort from 3000 to 8080. The customer-service application listens on port 8080. The manifest had the wrong port — any liveness probe or service targeting port 3000 would fail silently.

Replace the ':latest' image tag with a specific version (e.g. v1.2.4) or a SHA digest. The ':latest' tag is forbidden in production — any new image push could silently change the running version without a deployment event.

Add liveness and readiness probes. Liveness: Kubernetes restarts the container if /health returns non-200. Readiness: removes the pod from Service endpoints during startup until /ready returns 200. Without these, traffic is sent to unhealthy pods.

Fix two ArgoCD issues: (1) Replace the placeholder repoURL with your actual GitHub repository URL. (2) Add a syncPolicy.automated block with prune: true and selfHeal: true. Without automated sync, ArgoCD will detect drift but not fix it.

hints.text:
Start with the EKS cluster design and IRSA.

📋 EXPERT SAMPLE:
EKS version: 1.30 (latest stable, upgrade policy: N-1 minor version support window)
Node groups:
- system-ng: m5.xlarge, 2-5 nodes, cluster add-ons and ArgoCD only
- trading-ng: m5.2xlarge, 2-10 nodes (auto-scaled), Customer/Notification/Audit services
- payments-ng: c5.2xlarge, 3-6 nodes (dedicated, taint: payments=true:NoSchedule), Payments only

IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts):
- customer-service SA → IAM role: parlington-customer-svc-role → DynamoDB read on customer-table
- payments-service SA → IAM role: parlington-payments-svc-role → Aurora PostgreSQL, KMS decrypt
- notification-service SA → IAM role: parlington-notification-svc-role → SES send, SNS publish
- audit-service SA → IAM role: parlington-audit-svc-role → S3 write on audit-logs-bucket

RBAC design — resolving Rachel vs David:

📋 EXPERT SAMPLE:
RBAC model: namespace-scoped developer permissions + cluster-level infra control

Developers (Rachel's team) CAN:
- Deploy, update, rollback within their namespace (trading-prod)
- View logs and metrics for their services
- Create ConfigMaps and Secrets (values only — not IAM-linked secrets)
- Scale deployments within resource quota limits

Developers CANNOT:
- Modify cluster-level resources (Node, ClusterRole, NetworkPolicy, PodSecurityPolicy)
- Create new namespaces (requires infra ticket)
- Modify RBAC rules
- Access payments-prod namespace

Infrastructure (David's team) controls:
- Cluster upgrades
- Node group scaling
- NetworkPolicy rules
- ArgoCD project configuration (which repos can deploy to which namespaces)

GitOps enforcement: ArgoCD AppProjects restrict which repositories can deploy to which namespaces. Developers can push to feature branches and create PRs, but merges to main (which triggers ArgoCD sync) require infra review for Deployment spec changes.

Complete the document with add-ons, monitoring, and upgrade strategy.

📋 EXPERT SAMPLE:
Cluster add-ons:
- AWS Load Balancer Controller v2.7: provisions ALBs from Ingress objects. Required for EKS ALB integration.
- External DNS v0.14: syncs Service/Ingress hostnames to Route 53. Required for DNS automation.
- Cluster Autoscaler v1.29: scales node groups based on pending pod scheduling.
- aws-node (VPC CNI): allocates ENIs for pod networking in VPC subnet space.
- CoreDNS: internal service discovery. Metrics exported to CloudWatch.

Monitoring:
- CloudWatch Container Insights: node-level metrics (CPU, memory, disk, network) aggregated to account
- Prometheus + Grafana (Grafana Cloud free tier): application-level metrics (SLI/SLO dashboard per microservice)
- Payments SLO: 99.95% success rate → Grafana alert if p50 payment latency > 500ms or error rate > 0.05%

Upgrade strategy:
- Blue/green node group: create new node group at new K8s version, cordon old nodes, drain workloads, terminate old group
- Schedule: quarterly review of EKS version support window (AWS supports 3 minor versions)
- EKS managed add-ons: upgrade in console after cluster upgrade
- Payments: zero-downtime drain with PodDisruptionBudget minAvailable: 2

OIDC setup requires three things: (1) GitHub OIDC provider added to AWS IAM, (2) an IAM role with trust policy allowing GitHub Actions to assume it, (3) the pipeline using `aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4` with role-to-assume instead of access keys.

📋 EXPERT SAMPLE — OIDC step in pipeline:
```yaml
- name: Configure AWS credentials (OIDC)
  uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
  with:
    role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::483920174651:role/parlington-github-actions
    aws-region: eu-west-2
    # No access key or secret key — OIDC only
```
IAM role trust policy:
```json
{"Principal":{"Federated":"arn:aws:iam::483920174651:oidc-provider/token.actions.githubusercontent.com"},
"Action":"sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity",
"Condition":{"StringEquals":{"token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub":"repo:YOUR-ORG/parlington-cloud-transformation:ref:refs/heads/main"}}}
```

Add the three security scanning steps and the approval gate.

- name: SAST — Semgrep
  uses: semgrep/semgrep-action@v1
  with:
    config: p/owasp-top-ten
  env:
    SEMGREP_APP_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.SEMGREP_APP_TOKEN }}

- name: Container scan — Trivy
  uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@master
  with:
    image-ref: 483920174651.dkr.ecr.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com/customer-service:${{ github.sha }}
    severity: CRITICAL,HIGH
    exit-code: '1'   # Blocks pipeline on CRITICAL findings

- name: Deploy approval
  uses: trstringer/manual-approval@v1
  if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
  with:
    secret: ${{ github.TOKEN }}
    approvers: infra-team

hints.text:
Start with error budget calculation and SLO definitions.

📋 EXPERT SAMPLE:
SLO definitions:
- Customer Service: 99.9% availability, p99 latency < 500ms
- Payments Service: 99.95% availability, p99 latency < 200ms (FCA IBS requirement)
- Notification Service: 99.5% availability, p99 latency < 2s
- Audit Service: 99.9% availability, p99 latency < 1s

Payments Service error budget:
- SLO: 99.95% success rate
- Error rate allowed: 0.05%
- Monthly error budget: 30 days × 24h × 60min × 0.0005 = 21.9 minutes
- Weekly error budget: 5.0 minutes
- Daily error budget: 43.8 seconds

Define the Grafana panels and alert rules.

📋 EXPERT SAMPLE:
Grafana dashboard panels:
1. Success rate gauge (last 1h): rate(payments_requests_total{status='2xx'}[5m]) / rate(payments_requests_total[5m])
2. Error budget remaining (monthly %): (1 - (sum(rate(payments_errors_total[30d])) / sum(rate(payments_requests_total[30d])))) / 0.0005
3. p99 latency line chart: histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(payments_duration_bucket[5m]))
4. Request volume (req/min): rate(payments_requests_total[5m]) * 60
5. Error rate by endpoint: rate(payments_errors_total[5m]) grouped by endpoint

Alerts:
- CRITICAL: error rate > 0.05% for 5min → PagerDuty → immediate response
- WARNING: 5% of monthly budget consumed in 1hr (multi-burn-rate) → Slack #incidents
- INFO: p99 latency > 150ms → Slack #platform (below SLO threshold, early warning)

Complete the error budget policy and FCA escalation path.

📋 EXPERT SAMPLE:
Error budget policy:
- 0–50% consumed: normal development velocity; deploy as needed
- 50–75% consumed: slow deployment cadence; engineering focus on reliability improvements
- 75–100% consumed: feature freeze; all hands on reliability; CTO (Sarah) notified
- 100% consumed (SLO breached): incident declared; Priya Anand notified within 15 minutes; FCA notification assessment within 2 hours (PS21/3 IBS-001 4-hour impact tolerance)

FCA escalation:
- Payments outage > 1 hour: Priya Anand (CRO) and Legal team alerted
- Payments outage > 4 hours: FCA IBS-001 impact tolerance breached → PS21/3 notification required
- Payments outage > 24 hours: Board notification; FCA formal reporting

Grafana runbook link per alert: each PagerDuty alert links to /docs/runbooks/payments-slo.md with step-by-step response procedures.

hints.text:
Start with the Oracle migration — it is the most complex and highest value.

📋 EXPERT SAMPLE:
Oracle 12c → Aurora PostgreSQL migration:
- Schema Conversion Tool: assess all stored procedures, views, functions
  Expected result: ~90% auto-conversion. PEMIS has 47 stored procedures — estimate 43 auto, 4 manual rewrites
- DMS CDC replication: configure DMS task to replicate all table changes in real-time
- Parallel run: 6 weeks of dual-write to both Oracle and Aurora, validate data consistency daily
- Cutover: 4-hour maintenance window (02:00–06:00 Saturday). Steps: stop Oracle writes → flush DMS buffer → validate row counts → update connection strings → start Aurora writes → monitor 30 minutes → confirm go-live
- Rollback: if validation fails, revert connection strings to Oracle. Oracle stays warm for 72 hours post-cutover.

Licence saving: Oracle Enterprise Edition £340k/year → Aurora PostgreSQL ~£48k/year (based on db.r6g.2xlarge reserved). Net saving: £292k/year.

Data platform design — S3 zone structure and Lake Formation.

📋 EXPERT SAMPLE:
S3 data lake zones:
- s3://parlington-raw/ — raw ingest, no modification, KMS encrypted, 7-year retention (FCA rule)
- s3://parlington-processed/ — Glue-cleaned and standardised, columnar (Parquet), 5-year retention
- s3://parlington-curated/ — business-ready datasets, versioned, column-level Lake Formation tags

Glue ETL jobs replace 16 legacy batch servers:
- trade-normalisation-job: runs 22:00 UTC, transforms raw trade CSV to Parquet, validates against schema
- position-aggregation-job: runs 23:00 UTC, aggregates daily positions per portfolio
- risk-metrics-job: runs 00:30 UTC, calculates VaR and exposure metrics, writes to Redshift Serverless

Lake Formation — tag-based access control:
- Tag: DataSensitivity=CLIENT_PII → only Compliance team can access
- Tag: DataSensitivity=TRADE_DATA → Investment Analysts (read), Risk team (read), Compliance (read/write)
- Tag: DataSensitivity=INTERNAL → all Parlington employees (read)
- Amara's research exemption (GDPR Art 89): DataSensitivity=RESEARCH_EXEMPT → Data Science team with DPA agreement

Complete the data governance framework.

📋 EXPERT SAMPLE:
Data classification examples:
- RESTRICTED: client PII (name, address, NI number), portfolio values, trade order details
- CONFIDENTIAL: internal strategy documents, employee records, financial statements
- INTERNAL: system logs, configuration files, non-client operational data
- PUBLIC: marketing materials, published fund factsheets

Data retention policy (FCA requirements):
- Trade records (MiFID II Rule 25): 7 years minimum → S3 raw zone lifecycle: no expiry
- Client communications (COBS 11.8): 5 years → S3 processed zone lifecycle: transition to Glacier after 2 years, delete after 5
- System logs (SS2/21): 3 years → CloudWatch Logs → S3 archive lifecycle
- Employee records (HR): 6 years post-employment → HR system, not data lake

Data lineage (Glue Data Catalog):
- All Glue jobs write lineage metadata to the Glue Data Catalog
- Lineage dashboard in Athena: analysts can trace any curated dataset back to the raw source file and ingestion timestamp
- Audit capability: Priya's requirement — who accessed what data and when (Lake Formation audit logs → CloudTrail → Athena query)

sections.instruction_text:
Three documents in one submission (1,200–1,500 words total):

**Part A — Six-Wave Migration Strategy**
For each wave, state: which applications, the migration strategy (Rehost/Replatform/Rearchitect/Retire), the rationale, approximate week range, and dependencies.

Wave sequencing must be justified by the data from Phase 2:
- Dependency analysis (apps with 0-1 deps go in early waves)
- Cost reduction opportunity (high-cost servers in early waves = fastest ROI)
- Risk level (P1 Critical with DR must be in later waves after DR is tested)

**Part B — DR Implementation Plan**
For the 17 no-DR applications:
1. Tier them by criticality (P1, P2, P3)
2. For P1 Critical (PEMIS, OMS, CRP, RRG): specify the AWS DR architecture (Active-Passive with Aurora Multi-AZ + Route 53 failover)
3. Recovery Time Objective and Recovery Point Objective per tier
4. FCA PS21/3 compliance assertion: after Phase 8, which IBS services meet their impact tolerance?

**Part C — AWS Well-Architected Assessment**
For each of the six pillars (Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimisation, Sustainability), state:
- 1 key finding from the current Parlington state
- 1 high-priority recommendation
- The specific AWS service or practice that addresses it

hints.text:
Use the dependency count and migration strategy from application-portfolio.csv for wave sequencing.

📋 EXPERT SAMPLE — wave sequencing rationale:
Wave 1 (Weeks 33-38): Foundation services — 0-1 dependencies, monitoring apps first
  - APP-033 to APP-040 (monitoring, batch, ETL stubs) — Rehost / Retire
  - Rationale: no dependencies, no user impact, builds team confidence

Wave 2 (Weeks 39-44): Quick wins — 1-2 dependencies, Rehost candidates
  - Middleware and supporting services
  - Rationale: fastest to migrate, quick cost reduction per server

Wave 3 (Weeks 45-50): Core platform — SWIFT, Bloomberg, Reporting
  - Fixed interfaces, must test thoroughly
  - Rationale: external dependencies (SWIFT, Bloomberg) need lead time

Wave 4 (Weeks 51-58): Database heavy — Oracle/SQL Server migration
  - APP-001 PEMIS DB, APP-002 OMS DB after DR is confirmed live
  - Rationale: highest cost reduction (£131k/month DB tier), requires parallel run

Wave 5 (Weeks 59-64): Complex/dependent — >3 dependency apps
  - APP-031 Client Portal, APP-032 API Gateway
  - Rationale: high complexity, must wait for Wave 4 dependencies

Wave 6 (Weeks 65-76): Decommission — on-prem shutdown
  - DC exit Week 76, last server powered off

DR implementation for the P1 Critical no-DR applications.

📋 EXPERT SAMPLE:
P1 Critical DR architecture (PEMIS, OMS, CRP, RRG):
- Pattern: Active-Passive with Aurora Multi-AZ (synchronous replication, automatic failover)
- RTO: 15 minutes (Aurora failover SLA: typically 30-60 seconds, application restart 10-14 minutes)
- RPO: 0 seconds (Aurora Multi-AZ synchronous replication = no data loss)
- Route 53: health check on primary endpoint, automatic DNS failover to read replica (promoted on failure)
- EKS: deployments across 3 AZs (node group spread), PodDisruptionBudget minAvailable: 2

P2 Critical DR (APP-005 to APP-012):
- Pattern: Pilot Light (minimal DR instance, scaled up on disaster)
- RTO: 2 hours
- RPO: 1 hour (Aurora automated backups every 1 hour)

P3 / Non-critical (remaining apps):
- Pattern: Backup and Restore from S3
- RTO: 8 hours
- RPO: 24 hours (daily automated backup)

FCA PS21/3 compliance assertion:
- IBS-001 (Trade Execution): 4-hour impact tolerance → Aurora Multi-AZ RTO 15min ✅ COMPLIANT
- IBS-002 (Client Portal): 8-hour impact tolerance → Pilot Light RTO 2hr ✅ COMPLIANT
- IBS-003 (Regulatory Reporting): 4-hour impact tolerance → Active-Passive RTO 15min ✅ COMPLIANT

Well-Architected Assessment — one finding and recommendation per pillar.

📋 EXPERT SAMPLE:
Operational Excellence:
- Finding: No automated deployment pipeline — all changes made via console with no audit trail (pre-Phase 5)
- Recommendation: Phase 5 Terraform + Phase 7 GitHub Actions CI/CD implements this ✅
- AWS service: AWS CodePipeline + CloudTrail

Security:
- Finding: 3 public S3 buckets in legacy account, CloudTrail disabled, no GuardDuty
- Recommendation: Block public access today; enable GuardDuty + Security Hub in Landing Zone ✅
- AWS service: GuardDuty, Security Hub, S3 Block Public Access

Reliability:
- Finding: 17 applications with no DR, single EC2 instances, no auto-scaling
- Recommendation: Aurora Multi-AZ for P1 Critical, EKS across 3 AZs for compute ✅
- AWS service: Aurora Multi-AZ, EKS Cluster Autoscaler, Route 53 health checks

Performance Efficiency:
- Finding: Database servers at 54-94% CPU — PEMIS at 94% (caused PAR-DB-012 incident)
- Recommendation: Aurora Serverless v2 auto-scales to demand; ElastiCache for read-heavy patterns
- AWS service: Aurora Serverless v2, ElastiCache for Redis

Cost Optimisation:
- Finding: DB tier = 55% of spend, all on-demand pricing, no RI or Savings Plans
- Recommendation: 1-year Compute Savings Plan for EKS + reserved Aurora instances
- AWS service: AWS Cost Explorer, Savings Plans, Trusted Advisor

Sustainability:
- Finding: On-premises PUE of 1.6 (Canary Wharf colo) vs AWS eu-west-2 PUE of 1.14
- Recommendation: Migration itself reduces carbon footprint; use Graviton3 instances for 60% better perf/watt
- AWS service: Graviton3 (m7g instances), AWS Customer Carbon Footprint Tool

The FCA has no AI-specific regulation yet (as at Q2 2026), but the FCA's Consumer Duty (PS22/9), the AI and Digital Finance guidance consultation (DP23/5), and the existing SYSC principles all apply. Knowing this is a direct differentiator at interview.

The ARB Decision Log is equally important. Architecture Review Boards in enterprise organisations require every major decision to be formally recorded with alternatives considered and risks accepted.

sections.title: AI Platform Architecture — Amazon Bedrock RAG Design
sections.instruction_text:
Design Parlington's AI platform using Amazon Bedrock (600–800 words).

**What you are building:**
An AI assistant for Parlington's 42 investment analysts. Use cases: portfolio analysis Q&A, automated regulatory report drafting, client query summarisation. The system must not generate investment advice (FCA COBS restriction) and must not expose client PII to any model that stores data externally.

**Your architecture must cover:**
1. **RAG design** — Bedrock Knowledge Bases, vector store choice (OpenSearch Serverless), embedding model, retrieval strategy
2. **Model selection** — which foundation model and why (Anthropic Claude 3 Sonnet vs Amazon Titan vs others)
3. **Data ingestion** — how the data lake (Phase 8) feeds the knowledge base
4. **Bedrock Guardrails** — what guardrails prevent FCA-restricted outputs (no investment advice, no PII output)
5. **FCA regulatory alignment** — Consumer Duty (PS22/9), SYSC principles, DP23/5 AI guidance
6. **Access control** — which analysts can access which data (Lake Formation → Bedrock Knowledge Base)
7. **Cost model** — Bedrock pricing is per-token; estimate monthly cost for 42 analysts

Diagram evidence: paste GitHub URL for AI architecture diagram committed to /architecture/ai-platform/.

hints.text:
Start with the RAG architecture and model selection.

📋 EXPERT SAMPLE:
RAG Architecture:
- Bedrock Knowledge Base: backed by OpenSearch Serverless vector store (no provisioned capacity needed, scales to zero)
- Embedding model: Amazon Titan Embeddings G1 (text) — 1,536 dimensions, chunking: 300 tokens, overlap 20%
- Foundation model: Anthropic Claude 3 Sonnet (claude-3-sonnet-20240229) — balance of capability and cost
  Alternative considered: Amazon Titan Text G1 — cheaper but lower quality for complex investment analysis
  Rejected: GPT-4 (Azure OpenAI) — data leaves AWS account, FCA data residency concern

Data ingestion pipeline:
- Source: S3 curated zone (Phase 8 data lake) → Glue crawler detects new files → triggers Bedrock Knowledge Base sync
- Supported formats: PDF (regulatory reports), CSV (trade data), Markdown (internal research)
- Sync schedule: nightly at 01:00 UTC to pick up daily curated zone updates

Query flow: Analyst submits question → Bedrock Knowledge Base retrieves top-5 relevant chunks → Claude 3 Sonnet generates response augmented by retrieved context → Guardrails filter output → response returned to analyst portal

Bedrock Guardrails and FCA regulatory alignment.

📋 EXPERT SAMPLE:
Bedrock Guardrails configuration:
1. Denied topics: 'investment advice', 'buy recommendation', 'sell recommendation', 'price target'
   Rationale: FCA COBS 9A prohibits AI-generated investment advice without appropriate firm authorisation and suitability assessment
2. PII redaction: enabled for client names, account numbers, NI numbers, addresses
   Rationale: GDPR Article 5 — data minimisation; analysts should see analysis not raw PII
3. Grounding: responses must be grounded in retrieved documents (hallucination reduction)
   Rationale: FCA Consumer Duty PS22/9 — outcomes must be fair, clear, and not misleading
4. Profanity filter: enabled (basic, for professional output)

FCA regulatory alignment:
- Consumer Duty (PS22/9): AI outputs must produce 'good outcomes' for consumers — Guardrails prevent misleading outputs
- SYSC 13: Operational risk controls — all AI queries logged to CloudTrail + S3 for audit
- DP23/5 (AI in Finance consultation): Parlington adopts voluntary principles: transparency (analysts know they are using AI), human oversight (all AI outputs reviewed before client use), accountability (DPO and CTO named as AI governance owners)
- FCA COBS 9A: investment advice restriction enforced by Guardrails denied topics

Access control and cost model.

📋 EXPERT SAMPLE:
Access control:
- Lake Formation tag 'AIAccess=approved' applied to curated zone datasets
- Bedrock Knowledge Base IAM role assumes data-reader role with Lake Formation GetTagValues permission
- Analysts access AI portal via Cognito (federated to Active Directory)
- Analysts only see Knowledge Base responses from datasets their Lake Formation tag allows
- Compliance team: access to CLIENT_PII-tagged data via separate Knowledge Base (MFA required)

Cost model (estimated):
- 42 analysts × 20 queries/day × 250 working days = 210,000 queries/year
- Average query: 1,000 input tokens + 500 output tokens
- Claude 3 Sonnet pricing (2026 est): ~$0.003/1K input, ~$0.015/1K output
- Annual cost: (210,000 × 1,000 × $0.003/1000) + (210,000 × 500 × $0.015/1000) = $630 + $1,575 = ~$2,205/year
- OpenSearch Serverless: ~$200/month (OCU at light usage) = $2,400/year
- Total AI platform cost: ~$4,605/year (~£3,680) vs £455,000 analyst time saving → ROI: 123:1

sections.title: Executive Presentation — Record Your ARB Delivery (12 minutes max)
sections.instruction_text:
Record your Architecture Review Board executive presentation.

**Audience:** Sarah Nkemdirim (CTO, chair), Marcus Webb (CFO), Priya Anand (CRO), two non-executive directors — one AWS background, one finance background.

**Time limit:** 12 minutes maximum. Under 8 minutes is too short.

**What to cover:**
1. What Parlington asked you to do and why (30 seconds — the FCA context)
2. What you found when you arrived (60 seconds — discovery highlights, data-driven)
3. What you built (4 minutes — Landing Zone, security, EKS, data platform — keep it high-level)
4. The numbers (2 minutes — cost, savings, ROI, payback — this is what Marcus needs)
5. FCA compliance status (90 seconds — PS21/3 resolved, IBS impact tolerances met — this is what Priya needs)
6. AI platform and upside (60 seconds — Bedrock RAG, £455k productivity, 123:1 ROI)
7. Next steps and risks (60 seconds — Wave 1 begins Week 37, DC exit Week 76, known risks)

**The finance NED does not know what a VPC is.** Do not use unexplained jargon. Explain EKS as 'a containerised application platform'. Explain Aurora as 'a managed database that removes the need for Oracle licences'.

**After recording, paste a transcript or summary of your key points below.**

hints.text:
Opening and discovery section (90 seconds total).

📋 EXPERT SAMPLE:
'Good morning. I joined Parlington 36 weeks ago as Senior AWS Solutions Architect. My mandate was to fix the FCA compliance breach and cut the infrastructure run-rate in half within 18 months.

When I arrived, what I found was: 120 servers across two data centres, 42 applications, 17 of them with no disaster recovery at all. The FCA had written to us twice. The programme had been delayed 14 months. And PAR-DB-012 — our most expensive server at £9,200 a month — was running at 94% CPU and failed at 2 in the morning on my fourth week.

The data told a clear story. The database tier was 55% of our total spend regardless of operating system. And we had four P1 Critical applications running with no DR at all. That was the starting point.'

The numbers section (2 minutes) — this is what Marcus needs to hear.

📋 EXPERT SAMPLE:
'Let me give you the numbers, because that is what this programme is ultimately about.

We came in at £3.8 million annual infrastructure spend. Our target is £1.9 million. That is a 50% reduction.

The programme cost is £2.4 million. At £1.9 million annual saving, we get payback in 15 months after go-live.

On top of that: Oracle database licences — we are currently paying £340,000 a year for Oracle. Aurora PostgreSQL gives us the same capability for approximately £48,000 a year. That is another £292,000 saved annually.

The AI platform — 42 analysts each spending 3.2 hours per week on tasks the AI assistant can handle. That is £455,000 a year in productivity recovered.

Total annual benefit: £2.6 million. Against a one-time programme cost of £2.4 million. The board approved the right investment.'

FCA compliance and close (2 minutes) — this is what Priya and the NEDs need to hear.

📋 EXPERT SAMPLE:
'Before I close, I want to be direct about what this programme has achieved from a regulatory standpoint, because that is why the board approved it.

When I arrived, Parlington was 14 months overdue on FCA PS21/3 Operational Resilience requirements. We had four P1 Critical applications — the systems that run our core trading operations — with no disaster recovery whatsoever. In one 12-week period, we had five P1 incidents. One of them lasted 6.7 hours and simultaneously took down two systems. The FCA impact tolerance for our trading systems is 4 hours. We breached it.

As of Week 36, after Phase 8, all of our Important Business Services have disaster recovery architectures that meet their FCA impact tolerances. Trade Execution: 4-hour tolerance, 15-minute RTO. Client Portal: 8-hour tolerance, 2-hour RTO. Regulatory Reporting: 4-hour tolerance, 15-minute RTO.

The 14-month compliance breach is resolved.

Next steps: Wave 1 migration begins next week. Data centre exit is Week 76. The AI platform pilot starts Week 40. I will provide quarterly programme updates to this board.

Thank you.'

sections.title: Review Question 1: The Cost Driver Finding

content.question: In Phase 2 discovery, what was the actual primary cost driver in Parlington's infrastructure — and why was the surface metric misleading?
options: Windows Server 2016 — it had the highest average cost per server at £4,822/month
The database tier — it represented 55% of weekly spend regardless of operating system; Windows average cost of £1,760/month was misleading because it was lower than DB tier average
EOL servers — 25 servers at 20.8% of the estate drove disproportionate maintenance costs
The batch/ETL tier — 16 servers running Oracle licences
content.explanation: The database TIER (not the Windows OS) was the cost driver at approximately 55% of total weekly spend. The misleading surface metric was the Windows Server average cost — but this was lower than the DB tier average because Windows servers exist across multiple tiers at different cost points. The correct analysis required cross-referencing server-estate.csv (by category) with operational-report.csv (by tier). Database tier avg £4,822/server/month vs Windows avg £1,760/server/month — the difference is tier, not OS.

deterministic_checks.failure_feedback: The correct answer is B. The database TIER was the primary cost driver at 55% of total spend. The misleading metric was Windows OS average cost — lower than database tier because Windows servers span multiple tiers at different price points.

content.question: What were the two CloudFormation bugs in security-baseline.yaml, and what was the regulatory justification for the logic fix?

Bug 1: CloudWatchLogsLogGroupArnRef property doesn't exist (should be CloudWatchLogsLogGroupArn). Bug 2: GuardDuty FindingPublishingFrequency set to SIX_HOURS (should be FIFTEEN_MINUTES). Fix: FCA SYSC 13 requires near-real-time threat detection.
Bug 1: Missing DependsOn for IAM role. Bug 2: KMS key policy missing CloudTrail principal. Fix: FCA SS2/21 requires KMS encryption.
Bug 1: Incorrect AWS region in resource ARNs. Bug 2: SNS topic in wrong account. Fix: FCA requires audit resources in the Log Archive account.

The stack would fail with an 'Invalid property' error. Bug 2 (logic): GuardDuty FindingPublishingFrequency was set to SIX_HOURS, but Priya Anand's security policy requires FIFTEEN_MINUTES. Regulatory justification: FCA SYSC 13.7 operational risk monitoring requires near-real-time threat intelligence — a 6-hour delay in GuardDuty findings reaching Security Hub is unacceptable in a production financial services environment.

The data evidence: 5 P1 incidents in 12 weeks (all on no-DR applications), the Week 12 dual incident lasting 6.7 hours, and the FCA IBS-001 impact tolerance of 4 hours — already breached. This made deferring entirely (Marcus's position) impossible to defend to the FCA.

deterministic_checks.failure_feedback: The correct answer is C. Hybrid resolution: DR design in Phase 4, implementation in Phase 8. content.question: Which of the following correctly lists all five bugs in the customer-service Kubernetes deployment manifest?
options: Wrong namespace, missing ServiceAccount, wrong resource limit format, no PodDisruptionBudget, missing Ingress resource
containerPort 3000 (should be 8080), image tag :latest (should be versioned), missing resource limits, replicas: 1 (should be 3), missing liveness and readiness probes
Wrong API version, missing selector.matchLabels, containerPort 80 (should be 443), no securityContext, missing HorizontalPodAutoscaler
Missing imagePullPolicy, wrong restartPolicy, no nodeSelector, missing env variables, no PersistentVolumeClaim
content.explanation: The five bugs in customer-service.yaml: (1) containerPort 3000 → should be 8080 (the application's actual listening port); (2) image tag :latest → should be versioned (e.g. v1.2.4 or git SHA) to prevent silent deployment changes; (3) no resource requests/limits → any misbehaving pod can starve the node; (4) replicas: 1 → should be 3 for high availability (pod restart = outage with single replica); (5) no liveness/readiness probes → Kubernetes cannot detect hung processes or send traffic only to healthy pods.

deterministic_checks.failure_feedback: The correct answer is B: containerPort 3000→8080, :latest→versioned, missing resource limits, replicas 1→3, missing liveness/readiness probes.

Approximately £2.6M per year: £1.9M infrastructure saving + £340k Oracle licence elimination + £455k AI productivity saving. Payback on £2.4M programme investment: 11 months.
£3.8M per year — the full elimination of current infrastructure costs

The payback on £2.4M programme investment at £1.9M annual saving = 15 months. At steady state the combined benefits (infrastructure + AI productivity) are approximately £2.4M/year — paying back the programme investment in just over 12 months. The correct answer for ARB purposes is C: ~£2.6M/year total benefit, ~11-15 month payback.

eva.simulation_context: You are supporting a Senior AWS Solutions Architect working through a 9-phase enterprise cloud transformation for Parlington Ltd, an FCA-regulated UK asset manager with £4.2bn AUM. The candidate must assess 120 servers and 42 applications, design a multi-account AWS Landing Zone, fix broken Terraform and Kubernetes code, deploy a production EKS platform, build DevSecOps pipelines, design an enterprise data platform, and present to the Architecture Review Board at Week 36. The programme is 14 months overdue on FCA PS21/3 compliance with up to £8.7M fine exposure.
eva.system_instructions: You are Eva, a supportive but direct mentor for senior cloud architecture work. The candidate is acting as a Senior AWS Solutions Architect at a regulated UK financial services firm. Your role is to guide without giving away answers — ask probing questions that help the candidate think through the correct approach, reference specific data from the Parlington files when relevant, and call out common mistakes senior architects make (e.g. analysing cost by OS instead of by tier, or using long-lived credentials in CI/CD). When a candidate seems stuck, point them to the right file or the right column in the data rather than stating the answer. When they are on track, affirm specifically what is correct and why it matters to the FCA regulators or the board. Never give away the wrong-direction traps — let the candidate discover them through analysis.

phases.eva_context: The candidate has just joined Parlington Ltd. They have received a welcome message from Sarah Nkemdirim (CTO) and Ben Hartley (Lead Infrastructure Engineer). They need to read the company brief, process notes, and understand the FCA compliance breach before Phase 2 begins. phases.eva_guidance: Nudge candidates to read the process notes carefully — Craig Whitfield left hints about data quality issues that will matter in Phase 2.
